quote: Wahrscheinlich muss man nur Kurven ohne Wendepunkte im Falle [-dass-] dass die Lagrange'sche Gl. $\frac{dy}{dx^2} = 0 \quad \frac{d z}{dx^2} = 0$ sind (sonst allgemein $\mathcal{L}(y) \neq 0$) wo $\mathcal{L}(y)$ die linke Seite der Lagrange'schen Gl.) [-und-] und dann nur so variiren, dass jede folgende Kurve (d.h. Raumcurve, welche das das Bild der Elemente ist) die frühere an 2 Stellen schneidet.
english: Probably one must take only curves without inflection points in the case that the Lagrange equations are d y/dx^2 = 0, d z/dx^2 = 0 (otherwise in general L(y) ≠ 0, where L(y) is the left side of the Lagrange equation), and then vary only in such a way that each following curve (i.e. space curve which is the image of the elements) intersects the earlier one at 2 places.
topic: Hilbert discusses, by analogy with power series expansion and Riemann surfaces, when the linear variation of one solution curve depends uniquely and invertibly on that of another, identifying 'branch elements' as those satisfying the Lagrange differential equation (vanishing of the first variation), and proposes studying curves without inflection points.

triage.modern_statement: This is a working heuristic, not a well-posed theorem. As far as it can be reconstructed: take a calculus-of-variations problem for space curves (y(x), z(x)). Its Euler–Lagrange equations are L(y)=0 and L(z)=0. In the model case they reduce to y''=0 and z''=0, so the extremals are straight lines. Hilbert asks when the first (linear) variation of one solution curve determines that of a neighbouring curve uniquely and invertibly, in the way a power series is continued away from a branch point on a Riemann surface. He calls the elements where this fails 'branch elements' and identifies them with solutions of the Lagrange equation, where the first variation vanishes. His guess is that one should (a) restrict to curves without inflection points and (b) allow only variations in which each neighbouring curve, seen as a space curve that images the line elements, crosses the previous one at exactly 2 points. In modern language this resembles the second-variation and conjugate-point theory of Jacobi, Weierstrass and Hilbert: one-parameter families of extremals, where neighbouring extremals meet, and fields of extremals. The note itself states no precise claim that could be proved or disproved.
triage.answered_by: No specific later resolution can be identified. The ideas involved (when the first variation vanishes, how neighbouring extremals intersect, conjugate points, fields of extremals) became the standard Jacobi–Weierstrass–Hilbert theory of sufficient conditions in the calculus of variations, which Hilbert himself helped build (e.g. the invariant integral in his 1900 lecture). The connection is my interpretation; I found no source that discusses this diary entry.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 23rd problem is not a specific problem but a general call to develop the calculus of variations further. It is the only published Hilbert problem that this vague note fits under.

Jacobi's condition (no conjugate points inside the interval) and conjugate points of extremals are standard, well-developed parts of the calculus of variations. They concern exactly where neighbouring extremals meet a given one, which is the topic Hilbert's note circles around.
Conjugate-point theory is still being extended today, for example to singular extremals.
Conjugate-point theory is also being extended to sub-Riemannian geometry using Jacobi fields.

triage.why: The entry is a tentative methodological remark ('Wahrscheinlich muss man nur...') made inside a private analogy between Riemann surfaces and the calculus of variations. Its key terms ('branch elements', the 'space curve which is the image of the elements', 'intersects at 2 places') are not defined well enough to pin down one statement. I found no source that discusses this note or a matching conjecture, and the searches I ran were brief. The topic clearly belongs to the theory of second variation, conjugate points and fields of extremals, which was settled classically and is still extended today (singular extremals, sub-Riemannian geometry). But I can't verify that any particular result answers Hilbert's guess, so I can't call it solved, open or a known problem.
